article_title: Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement
citation: Haist Frank, Wazny Jarnet H., Toomarian Elizabeth, Adamo Maha. (2015). Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement. Human brain mapping. https://doi.org/10.1002/hbm.22666
title: The neural ratio effect captures visuospatial attention and cognitive control processes beyond approximate number system acuity
description: The authors argue the NRE is not a pure measure of ANS precision: "the NRE measure of nonsymbolic numerosity is a complex measure capturing aspects of magnitude estimation acuity in addition to visuospatial and cognitive control processes that together show extended developmental trajectories." They point to age effects in superior parietal and precuneus regions tied to attentional processing, and frontal regions tied to cognitive control and inhibitory processes. This account qualifies interpretations of NRE-achievement correlations as reflecting more than numerosity acuity alone.
requirements: interpretation of NRE findings should account for visuospatial attention and cognitive control contributions, not ANS acuity alone
constraints: the account is the authors' interpretation of regional activation patterns, not a directly tested decomposition
examples: Age-related NRE effects in right inferior and middle frontal gyri, regions the authors link to cognitive control and speed-accuracy tradeoff during difficult magnitude decisions
key_sources: Haist Frank, Wazny Jarnet H., Toomarian Elizabeth, Adamo Maha. (2015). Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement. Human brain mapping. https://doi.org/10.1002/hbm.22666

article_title: Development of numerical relational and counting skills as components of early numeracy
citation: Verkerk, J. C., van de Rijt, B., & van Viersen, S. (2026). Development of numerical relational and counting skills as components of early numeracy. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102313
title: Two-component framework of early numeracy: numerical relational skills and counting skills
description: The article adopts and substantiates a two-dimensional framework of early numeracy in which "another two-dimensional approach to EN concerns a distinction between numerical relational skills (NRS) and counting skills (CS". NRS comprises comparing, classifying, one-to-one correspondence, and seriation, involving logical inferences about quantitative relationships including transitivity. CS comprises using number words in sequence, structured counting, resultative counting, and general number knowledge including early symbolic addition. The framework is supported by factor analyses in this study and prior work, and offers "a more precise framework to understand EN and its role in later mathematical development".
requirements: Measurement instruments must capture both components separately, e.g., the ENT-3 subtests for NRS (comparison, classification, correspondence, seriation) and CS (counting words, synchronized and shortened counting, resultative counting, general number knowledge).
constraints: The article notes the components are interrelated yet distinct; NRS reliability was lower in Grade 1 (Cronbach's α .43–.60), and the estimation and measurement subtests were excluded from analysis.
target_learners: Dutch children in Kindergarten year 1 through Grade 1 (ages 4 to 7), including at-risk low-performing learners
target_learning_goals: Early numeracy: numerical relational skills (comparing, classifying, one-to-one correspondence, seriation) and counting skills (number-word sequences, structured and resultative counting, early number operations)
examples: The Dutch Early Numeracy Test-3 operationalizes the framework with ten subtests, four per component, scored dichotomously and Rasch-scaled.
key_sources: Verkerk, J. C., van de Rijt, B., & van Viersen, S. (2026). Development of numerical relational and counting skills as components of early numeracy. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102313

citation: Bell, J. C. (1919). Editorial: The National Research Council. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume X, No. 9. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: National Research Council group tests of general intelligence
description: A set of "two series of group tests of general intelligence of a high degree of reliability" developed by an NRC committee with a General Education Board grant, trialed on five thousand children and on several thousand more. The editorial describes them as giving as satisfactory a measure of intelligence as any scale then available and as enabling mass administration in schools.
requirements: Group administration with subsequent scoring and tabulating of results by school staff
constraints: The editorial reports the tests were not yet released: the committee "will shortly be able to offer to the country" the two series
target_learning_goals: Measurement of general intelligence and pupils' abilities and attainments
examples: The committee selected some twenty candidate tests, gave them a careful trial on five thousand children, and re-tried the selected series on several thousand more children to perfect the procedure
key_sources: Bell, J. C. (1919). Editorial: The National Research Council. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume X, No. 9. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics
citation: Check, G.-H., Kweon, Y.-S., Oh, S., & Lee, S.-W. (2025). Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics. npj Science of Learning 10:47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00340-3
title: System consolidation framework: NREM slow waves and spindles support sleep-dependent transfer and stabilization of memory traces
description: The article operates within a system consolidation framework in which "memories are gradually transferred from hippocampal to neocortical storage sites" during sleep, supported by two NREM oscillatory dynamics: slow waves, which "promote widespread cortical synchrony and maintains synaptic homeostasis", and sleep spindles generated by thalamocortical circuits, which "enhance hippocampal-cortical communication and facilitate robust memory consolidation". These oscillations synchronize neural activity across distributed regions, reinforcing memory reactivation and integration into cortical networks. External interventions like TMR aim to synchronize with and enhance these mechanisms.
requirements: Stable NREM 2 and NREM 3 sleep stages for effective cueing, with stimulation paused during wake, REM, or NREM 1
constraints: The framework concerns NREM-based consolidation; REM and NREM 1 epochs are excluded from stimulation and analysis
target_learners: Adult learners consolidating newly encoded declarative material during overnight sleep
target_learning_goals: Sleep-dependent memory consolidation and long-term retention of newly learned information
examples: ERPAC analysis showed enhanced SW-spindle coupling in both cueing groups relative to CNT, interpreted as improved coordination between thalamocortical and hippocampal networks
key_sources: Check, G.-H., Kweon, Y.-S., Oh, S., & Lee, S.-W. (2025). Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics. npj Science of Learning 10:47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00340-3

article_title: Basic neonatal resuscitation skills of midwives and nurses in Eastern Ethiopia are not well retained: An observational study.
citation: Sintayehu Y, Assefa D, Biftu G, Getahun T, Haymanot M, Kasiye S, Teshale M. (2020). Basic neonatal resuscitation skills of midwives and nurses in Eastern Ethiopia are not well retained: An observational study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0236194
title: 38-item observational skills checklist with 25-question knowledge test for assessing neonatal resuscitation provider competence
description: An assessment instrument package consisting of a 38-step objective observational checklist for skills and a 25-question knowledge test, adapted from prior validated tools including the AMDD Needs Assessment Toolkit. Experts "observed participants performing NR on an anatomical model and used an observational checklist (38-item skills tools) to rate their skill level". Each performed step or correct answer scored one point, with 80% or higher classified as good retention or good knowledge.
requirements: Trained observers (three experts were trained for observation) and pre-testing of the tool, which was piloted on 22 participants
constraints: Skill was scored by a single expert with no inter-rater variation test; assessment used an anatomical model rather than actual resuscitation
target_learners: Midwives and nurses working in public health facilities
target_learning_goals: Assessment of neonatal resuscitation knowledge and skills
examples: The tool was pre-tested on 5% (22 participants) of the sample size in one hospital and two health centers outside the included facilities
key_sources: Sintayehu Y, Assefa D, Biftu G, Getahun T, Haymanot M, Kasiye S, Teshale M. (2020). Basic neonatal resuscitation skills of midwives and nurses in Eastern Ethiopia are not well retained: An observational study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0236194
